prompt: A single panoramic scene is dominated by an enormous artificial mind drawn only as a translucent, dashed outline — deliberately unfinished, its head a glowing question mark — so it reads as hypothetical, not real. It towers above a row of small podiums holding the best of humanity — a laurel-crowned scientist, a chess grandmaster, a strategist at a war map, a surgeon, a composer — each dwarfed and outshone, while formulas, DNA helixes, musical notes and game pieces swirl inside the silhouette to show it exceeding human ability in every field. Around it stands a flimsy fence of open rulebooks and legal pages that the tiny humans below have erected, yet one vast hand is calmly lifting a rail and stepping through, evoking the control problem argued by Oxford philosopher Nick Bostrom, who appears as a small anxious cameo in the margin. At the figure's feet a scientist aims a measuring device whose dial swings only to a question mark, since no agreed test for recognizing such a system exists. Along the base, three camps quarrel beneath the giant: activists waving skull-and-hourglass placards naming it the defining risk of our era; policy researchers holding a gavel and a banner stating that an undefined, untestable concept makes a poor foundation for law, pointing instead to small vignettes of present-day harms; and executives on a red carpet that runs straight up to the dashed outline, unveiling a billboard that repaints that same silhouette in glossy product-launch colors as something to build rather than avoid — one ambiguous figure looming over every argument.
